name: Chorei
confidence_why: Jana 2025, a first-hand phonology of the Chorei variety with acoustic measurements, puts primary stress on the last syllable of the lexeme and finds no tone for most speakers, while the only other phonological descriptions, Borgohain & Khyriem 2022 and the Tezpur volume of 2021, treat the sister variety Sakachep/Khelma as tonal and say nothing about stress, so the record rests on a single strong source with no direct contradiction.
catalog_citation: Jana, Dibyajyoti. 2025. Phonology of Chorei, A Tibeto-Burman Language of Northeast India. Research MA thesis (Linguistics), Leiden University (supervisors M. Klamer, L. Konnerth). Open Access,https://hdl.handle.net/1887/4257879
catalog_locator: Ch. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology', section 4.1 'Stress', pp. 51-53; restated in ch. 5 Conclusion p. 55 and as phonological-word criterion 1 in section 3.2 p. 49; absence of tones section 4.2 pp. 53-54
catalog_quote: Each Chorei content word has one primary stress. The existence of stress in Chorei is confirmed by its effects on the word-structure, e.g. pre-tonic vowel deletion (§2.4.2) and shortening of vowels in unstressed open syllables (§2.4.4), which are both typical of stress systems (Kager 2007, 195, 198). The primary stress in Chorei words lies on the last syllable of the lexeme. Usually, this is the root of the word, as the commonest Chorei derivational morphology is prefixal (§3.1). However, when a derivational suffix occurs, it receives the stress, e.g. dông-mâ /dɔːŋˈmaː/ ‘family-FEM > wife’. In contrast, inflectional suffixes, e.g. -â /aː/ ‘LOC’, are normally unstressed, e.g. ray-â /ˈra.jaː/ ‘axe-LOC > on the axe’. Prefixes, whether derivational or inflectional, are never stressed. In Chorei, the most reliable correlate of stress is intensity. The stressed syllable is louder than the others in the word. It is also somewhat longer in duration than a corresponding unstressed syllable. ... The occurrence and characteristics of secondary stress in Chorei is currently not well-understood, since most Chorei lexemes are only one or two syllables long. ... all syllables lacking primary stress have been treated as unstressed. [p. 51] ... Each Chorei lexeme has a prominent lexical stress on its last syllable which is usally its root, but may be a derivational suffix. Inflectional affixes/clitics generally appear to be unstressed. [p. 55]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (lexeme) stress is fixed on the final syllable of the lexical stem: the last root syllable, or a derivational suffix if one follows; prefixes (derivational or inflectional agreement proclitics) are never stressed and inflectional suffixes/enclitics (e.g. locative -â, plural -ngay, nominalizer -nâ) normally fall outside the stress domain, so in fully inflected words stress is stem-final rather than strictly word-final. Main acoustic correlate is intensity, secondarily duration. The language (as spoken by most speakers in Manikbond) has no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'The occurrence and characteristics of secondary stress in Chorei is currently not well-understood'; non-lexeme-final lexical roots in compounds (e.g. kê in kê-kadoy /(ˌ)keː.kaˈdɔj/, dông in dông-mâ) are possible bearers of secondary stress (they keep length contrast in closed syllables and can trigger vowel harmony), but this could not be confirmed, so all syllables without primary stress are treated as unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal negative suffixes -mak 'NFUT.NEG', -nô 'FUT.NEG', -loy '?.NEG' attract stress although expected to be inflectional (ni-ˈmak, sa-ˈloy, with shortening of the root vowel); nominalizer -nâ stays unstressed although derivational-like; grammaticalizing -(n)zay 'PFV' is variably stressed (a-ˈkang-zay vs a-hek-ˈzay); status of postposed grammatical words such as comparative naykin (separate phonological word vs. phrase-final intonational prominence) unresolved.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexeme/phonological word ('Each Chorei content word has one primary stress'); based mainly on a c. 1000-item wordlist elicited from four speakers plus limited connected speech, Manikbond village (Assam, near Tripura/Mizoram border), Feb-Apr 2025; author notes higher-level prosody is not yet analysed. NOTE the variety: this is Chorei (Glottolog dialect chor1278 of saka1283 'Sakachep-Chorei'), not Khelma/Sakachep proper, for which the two accessible phonologies (Borgohain & Khyriem 2022; Bhattacharyya & Dutta 2021 per editorial summary) report lexical tone (3 resp. 2 tones) and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes CHOREI (Glottolog dialect-level code chor1278, listed under saka1283 'Sakachep-Chorei', ISO sch), as spoken in Manikbond village, Assam (Tripura/Mizoram border), which its speakers and the author treat as a distinct but mutually intelligible variety alongside Sakachep/Khelma, Ranglong and Hrangkhol. For KHELMA/SAKACHEP proper (Dima Hasao, Barak Valley, Meghalaya; dialects Hanle and Hante per the 2017 learner's book) the accessible descriptions are tonal and silent on stress: Borgohain & Khyriem 2022 (NEHU) report three register tones (high/mid/low); Bhattacharyya & Dutta 2021 (Tezpur CFEL, not online) reportedly two lexical tones. Jana 2025 finds Chorei NON-tonal with lexeme-final stress, so the prosodic description may not transfer to Sakachep proper; a catalog entry should be labelled 'Chorei (chor1278)' or flagged as dialect-specific.

new_statements.quote: Five vowels and two diphthongs are generally regular across the five KC languages of Barak valley. These vowels show distinctive length except in open syllables where the vowel naturally surfaces as long unless occurring as the unstressed initial syllable of a disyllabic compound. In Chorei, the minimal pair for e vs. ee is not found in a closed syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Jana 2025: primary stress on the last syllable of the lexeme; pre-tonic reduction): Haokip's remark that the initial syllable of a disyllabic compound is unstressed and its vowel not long points the same way (non-initial prominence). Adds nothing on placement beyond that. Potential tension not verifiable from the snippet: Haokip frames all five Barak Valley KC languages as tonal (section 4), whereas Jana 2025 section 4.2 finds no lexical tone in Chorei; the visible tone examples are for Saihriem, Ranglong and Hrangkhol only, so no Chorei tone claim can be quoted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Incidental remark only: in the five Barak Valley Kuki-Chin languages (Chorei and Sakachep included) the initial syllable of a disyllabic compound is unstressed (i.e. prominence on the non-initial/main syllable); the paper's prosodic sections (3 'Prosodic phonology', 4 tones) treat these languages as tonal, with tone inventories visible in the snippet only for Saihriem, Ranglong and Hrangkhol. Whether the full text states a stress rule or a tone inventory for Chorei/Sakachep specifically cannot be seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Haokip 2019 treats Chorei and Sakachep as two of five Kuki-Chin varieties of Barak Valley (Cachar/Hailakandi, Assam), both filed under saka1283 (Glottolog: Chorei = dialect chor1278 of Sakachep [sch]); the catalog record rests on Jana 2025, which describes the Chorei variety of Manikbond, Assam.

readall_conflicts: A standing tension already held by the project (not from the listed work): Jana 2025 (Chorei variety, Manikbond, Assam) finds a stress system with final primary stress and no phonological tone (sec. 4.2 'Absence of tones', pp. 53-54, with only one elderly speaker producing possible tonal contrasts), whereas Borgohain & Khyriem 2022 (Sakachep, NEHU MA extract, sec. 4.4) describe three phonemic register tones (high, mid, low) and say nothing about stress, and the Tezpur CFEL editorial note says Khelma has two contrastive lexical tones. These concern different named varieties (Chorei vs Sakachep/Khelma) under the same Glottolog language, so they may be dialect differences or analytical differences; Haokip 2019, unread, is exactly the comparative source that could settle.

sources.note: Ch. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology', 4.1 Stress (p. 51-53): every content word has one primary stress, on the last syllable of the lexeme (usually the root; a derivational suffix if present takes it); inflectional suffixes normally unstressed, prefixes never stressed; main correlate intensity (+ some duration); evidence from pre-tonic vowel deletion and unstressed open-syllable vowel shortening; secondary stress on non-final roots possible but unconfirmed; negative suffixes -mak/-no/-loy attract stress. 4.2: tones absent for most speakers (one elderly speaker produced unverified pitch contrasts).
